01The question

Can we see decay coming, instead of reacting to it?

Content teams usually refresh pages months after traffic has already dropped. The question behind this project: can historical search signals, exposure volume, and how stale a page is predict that a page is about to decay — early enough to act?

Decision this supports

Instead of reactive refreshes, editorial teams get a ranked list of high-exposure pages showing pre-decay risk, so updates and intent re-alignment can be scheduled ahead of the drop rather than after it.

02The data

30,000 pseudonymized content items, one honest exclusion

Each row is a content item — a pseudonymized content_id — tracked across client tenants. Items still labeled "new" aren't comparable to established content, so they were dropped before anything else. The target is simple: did this page's trend direction turn down.

03Methodology

The split is where most decay models quietly cheat

A page's own recent clicks and impressions are the decay — using them as inputs would just be predicting the label with itself. Every 90-day, 30-day, and rate-derived metric describing current performance was excluded, leaving only pre-decay signals: search demand, content attributes, and freshness.

What went in

23 features: search volume & competition, word/char count, content type & intent, provider/model used to produce it, prior-30-day exposure (impressions_prev_30d), content age, and days since last update.

What was excluded on purpose

All 90-day and last-30-day outcome metrics, CTR, average position, engagement/scroll rate, AI-traffic share, and any pre-binned tier built from those — 21 columns, all direct leakage.

The split

Grouped by client_id, not row — 24 clients train, 7 clients held out completely. The model is tested on accounts it has never seen a single page from.

The model

LightGBM classifier, 150 trees, depth 5, shallow and regularized on purpose — this is a scoring signal for humans to triage, not an autonomous decision-maker.

04Results vs. baseline

Beats the team's heuristic — the heuristic barely beats a coin flip

Three things were compared on the exact same unseen-client split: always predicting decay, the existing "stale + no ranking" rule of thumb, and the leakage-checked model.

Worth noting honestly: the heuristic scores below the random baseline on AUC — its ranking is actively worse than chance, even though raw accuracy looks close. Accuracy alone would have hidden that.

05What drives the prediction

Exposure and staleness carry the signal — not the writing itself

Ranked by split count, the model leans hardest on how much prior exposure a page had and how long it's gone untouched. Word count and content age matter; provider/model metadata barely register.

06Limitations

What this model can't claim

On the 5,592-item unseen-client test set, the error profile is close to balanced — it doesn't over-index toward false alarms or missed risk in one direction.

1,040 / 5,592

False positives — pages flagged for an audit that wasn't actually needed. Wasted editorial time, not a broken page.

989 / 5,592

False negatives — real decay the model missed. This is the costlier failure mode: risk that goes unflagged.

An AUC of 0.688 is directional, not diagnostic — it ranks pages by decay risk well enough to prioritize a review queue, not well enough to auto-action anything. Claims here are observed and measured on this split only; they haven't been validated against a live, deployed refresh workflow.
